claims.text: Reducing PtPdRhRuIrOs particle size increases the proportion of high-index facets relative to low-index facets.
A higher proportion of high-index facets alters the local electronic structure of the catalyst surface.
The altered electronic structure enhances adsorption and desorption kinetics of ethanol and its intermediates.
Enhanced adsorption and desorption kinetics improve ethanol-oxidation activity.
Enhanced adsorption and desorption kinetics improve catalyst durability during ethanol oxidation.
The baseline PtPdRhRuIrOs solid-solution catalyst has an average particle size of approximately 3 nm.
The baseline catalyst has a defined distribution of crystal facets.
The proposed intervention is to prepare PtPdRhRuIrOs particles with average sizes of 5–7 nm using a modified polyol reduction method.
Particle size directly controls the ratio of exposed high-index to low-index sites.
High-index facets provide distinct electronic environments and active-site densities that optimize intermediate adsorption and desorption.
Larger particles have a different facet distribution that changes reaction-intermediate adsorption and desorption kinetics.
Changing from approximately 3 nm particles to 5–7 nm particles will produce measurable differences in catalytic activity and durability.
The particle-size-dependent mechanism is expected to apply within approximately 3–7 nm for modified-polyol PtPdRhRuIrOs catalysts in 0.1 M HClO4–ethanol electrolyte.
Support interactions and local adsorbate effects may influence the quantitative relationship between high-index-facet fraction and catalytic performance.
An absence of statistically significant activity, durability, or selectivity differences between 3 nm and 5–7 nm samples would falsify the proposed particle-size-dependent facet mechanism.

contradictions.description: The larger particles are to be produced using a modified polyol method, while the baseline is described as synthesized under identical conditions. If synthesis is modified to control size, the two preparations are not literally identical.

The experiment intentionally changes particle size from approximately 3 nm to 5–7 nm, yet it proposes verifying that the only significant difference is facet distribution. Particle size itself necessarily remains a significant difference.
